cim_eredeti: Utah lets AI renew—and in one pilot write—prescriptions, but federal FDA oversight remains unanswered
szoveg_eredeti:
The Department of Health and Human Services released a roadmap to speed the use of artificial intelligence in clinical care, but it does not say whether the Food and Drug Administration is overseeing Utah's pilot programs that let AI renew and, in one case, write prescriptions, Nextgov reported Nov. 16.

The FDA generally requires premarket authorization for software that can diagnose or treat patients, and Utah's pilots involve that kind of technology. FDA officials have not said whether they are regulating the tools being tested in Utah.

For patients, the gap is about accountability. Utah residents can now get some prescriptions renewed or issued by AI systems for a few dollars, and the question of which agency checks those systems before and after launch has no clear federal answer.

The roadmap calls for clinical AI to meet a "better than today" standard for safety and effectiveness.

Its proposals include partnering with state-level regulatory sandboxes, writing risk-based rules, expanding outcomes-based payments, improving health data sharing, monitoring AI tools after they reach the market, and clarifying who is liable when AI harms a patient. Liability is listed as something HHS plans to help clarify, not something the roadmap resolves.

The document also says the federal government wants to work with states to address areas of clear state regulation, without explaining what that covers, Nextgov reported. States license clinicians and regulate the practice of medicine, while the FDA regulates medical devices, including some software.

Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy said it is actively coordinating with federal partners so state efforts align with federal frameworks. A senior Utah AI official had earlier declined to speak for the FDA.

Utah's Office of AI Policy, launched in 2024, can grant companies temporary regulatory relief to test AI tools in exchange for monthly reports, and it can require changes or end a pilot, according to Becker's Hospital Review.

The first pilot, with the company Doctronic, was approved in October 2025 and announced publicly Jan. 6 under a one-year agreement that the state may renew, according to the Utah Department of Commerce. Its AI can renew refills for 192 common medications for chronic conditions but cannot issue new prescriptions, change treatment plans, or renew controlled substances. In its first phase, a licensed clinician must authorize every request, and the pilot remained in that phase as of Becker's latest update. Approved renewals must be marked as AI-generated, Drug Topics reported.

Other pilots followed. Legion Health was approved in April for a 12-month pilot to refill common psychiatric medications. August AI was approved for chronic medication renewals at $4 per refill. Nolla Health, approved Oct. 5, says it is the first U.S. company cleared for AI to write new prescriptions for acne treatments chosen from a physician-approved list, at $4.99 a month.

Early results are limited. In Doctronic's first months, the AI recommended renewal in 72% of cases and physicians agreed 91% of the time, Becker's reported. Physicians judged about a third of the cases the AI sent to humans as overly cautious. No serious safety incidents had been reported.

Critics have pushed back. In April, Utah's Medical Licensing Board asked the state to halt the Doctronic pilot, citing patient safety and saying it had not been consulted, according to a Becker's explainer on the Utah pilot. The state's AI policy office declined but said it would modify or cancel the program if safety benchmarks were not met.

Researchers have also raised safety concerns and questioned whether the tools need FDA approval. A third-party review flagged potential vulnerabilities under deliberate misuse, and the state has said hard stops block unauthorized dispensing of controlled substances.

The state has made changes along the way. The headache medicine butalbital and the heart rhythm drug flecainide were removed from Doctronic's list, according to the Commerce Department. Zach Boyd, who heads Utah's AI office, has said Doctronic has so far been overly cautious, often sending uncontroversial decisions to doctors, the Associated Press reported.

The stakes extend beyond Utah. Doctronic is reportedly in talks to expand to Arizona, Missouri, Texas, and Wyoming, Becker's reported.

Patients who use an AI refill or prescribing service can ask whether a licensed clinician reviews its decisions, how to reach a person with questions, and what happens if the AI declines a request. Utah requires pilot companies to disclose AI use, carry malpractice insurance, and keep 24-hour incident response plans.

Sharing a full medication list and medical records helps any prescriber, human or AI, catch interactions. In May, Utah's AI policy office recommended that the Doctronic pilot strongly encourage, but not require, patients to share health records before a renewal. Patients should tell their regular doctor about prescriptions they receive through any app.

New side effects such as rash, swelling, dizziness, chest pain, or trouble breathing after a refill need prompt medical attention. Suspected problems with a medicine can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch program.

Utah has said pilot data will be shared publicly. MedicalDaily will report on any FDA statement about oversight of the pilots.

What did HHS release? A roadmap to speed clinical AI through state sandboxes, risk-based rules, outcomes-based payment, and post-market monitoring.

Does the roadmap say whether FDA oversees Utah's pilots? No. FDA officials have not said whether they regulate the Utah tools.

What can Utah's AI tools do? Some renew refills for chronic medications. One pilot lets AI write new acne prescriptions.

Is a doctor involved? In early phases, clinicians review AI decisions. Oversight is designed to decrease over time with state approval.

Have there been safety problems? No serious incidents have been reported, but critics have raised safety and oversight concerns.

What should patients ask? Whether a clinician reviews decisions, how to reach a person, and how to report a problem.
cim: Az USA-ban már receptet is írhat az AI, de tisztázatlan a szabályozás
lead: Utah államban kísérleti jelleggel mesterséges intelligencia újíthat meg és írhat fel gyógyszereket, miközben a szövetségi felügyelet még bizonytalan.
osszefoglalo:
Az amerikai Egészségügyi Minisztérium új útmutatót adott ki a klinikai mesterséges intelligencia használatának felgyorsítására. A dokumentum ugyanakkor nem tisztázza, hogy az Élelmiszer- és Gyógyszerengedélyezési Hivatal (FDA) felügyeli-e azokat a kísérleti programokat, amelyekben algoritmusok gyógyszerrecepteket írnak fel vagy hosszabbítanak meg.

Utah államban több cég is engedélyt kapott AI-alapú rendszerek tesztelésére. A Doctronic rendszere krónikus betegségek 192-féle gyógyszerét tudja meghosszabbítani, míg a Nolla Health megoldása új recepteket is kiadhat akne kezelésére egy előre jóváhagyott listáról. A kísérletek első fázisában orvosoknak kell ellenőrizniük a döntéseket, az állam pedig havi jelentéseket követel meg a cégektől.

Bár súlyos biztonsági incidens nem történt, a helyi orvosi kamara és szakértők aggályaikat fejezték ki a betegbiztonság és a szövetségi engedélyek hiánya miatt. A Doctronic adatai szerint az algoritmus az esetek 72 százalékában javasolta a megújítást, és az orvosok a döntések 91 százalékával egyetértettek. A rendszer jelenleg terjeszkedést tervez más amerikai államokba is.
miert_szamit: Ez a gyakorlat azt mutatja, hogy az AI-alapú döntéshozatal már az **erősen szabályozott egészségügyben** is utat tör magának. Az állami tesztkörnyezetek (sandboxok) modellje mintaként szolgálhat más iparágak számára is a kockázatos AI-alkalmazások piaci bevezetéséhez.

prioritas.indok: Fontos egészségügyi AI alkalmazás és szabályozási kérdéskör egy államban. Forrás-tapasztalat: -6.
prioritas.cim_hu: AI írhat fel vényre kapható gyógyszereket Utah államban
prioritas.lead_hu: Egy tesztprogram keretében már mesterséges intelligencia is megújít és kiír receptet, ám az FDA felügyelete még bizonytalan.

tenyellenorzes.esemeny: Az amerikai Egészségügyi Minisztérium (HHS) útmutatót adott ki az AI klinikai alkalmazásának felgyorsítására, de a dokumentum nem tisztázza az FDA felügyeleti jogkörét Utah állam kísérleti programjai felett, ahol az AI már gyógyszereket újíthat meg és írhat fel.
